summary: Records the 2003 discussions of the Problem working group on how to address the problems in the IETF Problem Statement. It breaks each problem into areas for improvement and sorts them into those affecting routine standards processes and those concerning the organization itself.

plainLanguage.summary: A club writes down what is going wrong with how it works and sorts the problems into piles so it can fix them one by one.

subtitle: How the IETF analyzed and began to fix its organizational problems

tldr.problem: By 2003, the IETF was struggling with organizational and process problems including unclear mission, ineffective engineering practices, difficulty handling complex issues, management scaling problems, and insufficient participant engagement.
tldr.mechanism: The Problem Working Group analyzed each of the seven root problems, decomposed them into areas for improvement, and separated them into routine process improvements that could be done immediately and structural changes requiring deeper organizational redesign.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends near-term improvements to working group quality, tools, training, and communication, while delegating longer-term structural questions to the IESG. It balances the need for improvement with respect for the IETF's core values and existing successful work.

today: RFC 3844 is an Informational RFC that documents the IETF's self-assessment and improvement planning from 2003. Many of the recommended routine improvements have been pursued by the IETF over subsequent years, including better tooling, expanded training programs, and more transparent working group practices.

sections.title: The IETF's Challenge
sections.content:
By 2003, the IETF had produced many of the world's most important internet standards, but the organization faced significant operational challenges. The Problem Statement RFC 3774 identified seven root problems: lack of shared mission understanding, inconsistent engineering practices, difficulty with complex problems, misuse of the three-step standards process, workload exceeding engaged participants, management structure not scaled to the organization's size, working group practices hindering issue closure, and inadequate leader preparation.

This RFC records the discussions of the Problem Working Group and proposes solutions. The IETF's core values—caring for the internet, technical competence, open process, volunteer core, and rough consensus—must be preserved while improvements are made.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF makes the rules for the internet, but by 2003 the rule-making process itself had problems. Too many chiefs, not enough focus, meetings dragged on. The group sat down and listed what needed fixing.

sections.title: The IETF's Core Values and Success
sections.content:
The IETF's mission is to produce high-quality, relevant, and timely technical standards for the internet. The organization's core values are: Cares for the Internet, Technically Competent, Open Process, Volunteer Core, and Rough Consensus and Running Code.

The RFC emphasizes that the IETF has been remarkably successful despite its current problems. Many things that might seem inflexible—the division into working groups and areas, the three-step standards process, the ASCII format for documents, the structure of meetings and mailing lists—are not core to the IETF's mission. These are non-core values that can be changed if they no longer serve the goals.

The document cautions against overreacting to problems with sweeping revolutionary changes. The IETF should focus on continuous improvement while protecting the valuable work already underway and the talented people leading it.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF is good at what it does. It cares about the internet, it is technically smart, it is open, it runs on volunteers, and it goes with the flow. Those five things matter. Everything else can change if needed.

sections.title: Decomposing the Problems
sections.content:
The RFC analyzes each of the seven root problems and breaks them into smaller areas for improvement. The analysis reveals two categories: routine process improvements that are independent and can be addressed immediately with minimal disruption, and structural issues that are interdependent and affect how the IETF fundamentally operates.

For example, the Mission Problem requires articulating the IETF's shared understanding of its mission, scope, goals, and stakeholders. The Engineering Practices Problem involves four areas: clearly defining work scope and acceptance criteria, implementing issue tracking and change control, ensuring quality throughout development, and recognizing timely execution. The Management Scaling Problem notes that IESG members are overloaded, leadership comes from a small pool, and one or two people can indefinitely block work.
sections.plainLanguage: Each big problem breaks into smaller pieces. Some pieces are independent and easy to fix now. Others are tangled together and need a bigger rethink.

sections.title: Immediate Improvements to Routine Processes
sections.content:
The RFC recommends five high-priority near-term improvements, each largely independent and unlikely to be invalidated by future structural changes: First, improve working group quality processes through a dedicated WG focused on chartering, quality processes, and review effectiveness. Second, increase the availability and use of issue tracking and document revision control tools. Third, improve training for IETF leaders and participants. Fourth, encourage direct communication between working group chairs to identify and resolve multi-WG issues rather than routing everything through the IESG. Fifth, develop better mechanisms to maintain IETF standards.

The IESG should also consider internal process changes to prevent one or two members from indefinitely blocking documents, to delegate more responsibility to working group chairs and directorates, to broaden the working group chair selection process, and to conduct regular reviews of milestones and progress.
sections.plainLanguage: Fix five easy things first: make working groups run better, use computers to track issues, train the leaders, let the chairs talk directly to each other, and maintain old standards better.

sections.title: Structural Change and the Path Forward
sections.content:
Major structural changes to the IETF's mission understanding, complex problem handling, standards hierarchy, management scaling, and engagement would require a more integrated approach. The Problem Working Group considered several processes for developing solutions: a dedicated General Area WG, a Strategy and Answers Panel of delegated representatives, a team of wise people appointed by the IESG, or IESG-led development.

Without consensus on the best approach, the RFC falls back to recommending that the IESG take responsibility for controlling the development of structural solutions where it believes they are necessary. The RFC also cautions that evolutionary proposals are more likely to be acceptable than revolutionary changes, and any transitions must be orderly.
sections.plainLanguage: The hard problems (how the IETF is run, how decisions are made) need deeper thought. No one agreed on the best way to fix them, so the IETF's leaders (IESG) will figure it out.

sections.title: Building the Future
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that the IETF must work to solve its problems both through focused immediate improvements and through a careful, integrated effort to build organizational structures and processes that handle the IETF's current scale and complexity. However, any major structural changes must preserve the IETF's mission and core values.

The Problem Working Group could not reach consensus on processes for addressing structural problems, which the RFC acknowledges may be typical for the IETF when discussing high-level concepts rather than concrete technical proposals. The RFC emphasizes that improvements should not block ongoing work on specific solutions, such as discussions about revising the standards maturity levels.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF has what it takes to fix itself. Work on quick improvements now. Think hard about the bigger changes. Keep doing the good work that matters.

viz.caption: Seven root problems decomposed into improvement areas
Two parallel paths to IETF improvement

items.title: Near-term improvements
items.text: Independent, addressable now with minimal disruption. Examples: better tools, training, document tracking, chair communication.

items.title: Structural changes
items.text: Interdependent, require deeper redesign. Examples: mission alignment, management scaling, standards process revision.
